body.statement: For every \(n\ge2\), the construction \(\mathfrak H_n^{\mathrm{comp}}\) yields deterministic numbers \(0<\ell\le h\le1\), amplitudes \(a,b>0\), and two finite priors \(\Pi_+\) and \(\Pi_-\), supported on \(\mathcal P(d,\alpha,\beta,\gamma,L)\), under each of which \(\tau_P(0)\) is constant, such that their constants differ by at least \(c\rho_n\) and the genuine fixed-\(n\) observed-data product mixtures have squared Hellinger distance at most \(1/4\).  More precisely, the singleton conditional sign-mixture laws are equal; if \(Q_{r,+}\) and \(Q_{r,-}\) denote the two conditional sign-mixture laws on any dependency component of size \(r\ge2\), then \[H^2(Q_{r,+},Q_{r,-})\le Ca^2b^2r^4(9/2)^r,\] and the full mixtures satisfy \[H^2\!\left(\int P_O^{\otimes n}\,d\Pi_+,\int P_O^{\otimes n}\,d\Pi_-\right)\le Cn^2h^d\ell^da^2b^2\le\frac14.\]  The construction keeps \(P_X\) exactly uniform on the full cube and uses neither an occupancy conditioning event nor Poissonization.
body.proof_tex:
Put \(D=[0,1]^d\) and \(p=3/8\).  We first construct the two priors at an arbitrary fixed point \(x_\circ\in D\); taking \(x_\circ=0\) proves the displayed claim, while taking \(x_\circ=x_0\) gives the same certificate at the fixed target point from \(\mathrm{def:component\mbox{-}handle}\).

We use two explicit smooth building blocks.  Define
\[
 U(t)=e^{-1/t}\mathbf 1_{\{t>0\}},\qquad
 R(t)=\frac{U(t)}{U(t)+U(1-t)},\qquad
 \kappa(t)=R(2-2|t|).
\]
The denominator defining \(R\) is strictly positive on \(\mathbb R\).  The function \(U\), with all derivatives set equal to zero on \(( -\infty,0]\), is \(C^\infty\); quotient differentiation therefore shows that \(R\) is \(C^\infty\), equals zero on \(( -\infty,0]\), and equals one on \([1,\infty)\).  Although \(|t|\) is not differentiable at zero, \(\kappa\) is identically one on a neighborhood of zero.  Away from zero it is a composition of smooth functions, and flatness of \(R\) at zero and one matches the pieces at \(|t|=1/2\) and \(|t|=1\).  Hence \(\kappa\in C^\infty(\mathbb R)\), \(0\leq\kappa\leq1\), \(\kappa=1\) on \([-1/2,1/2]\), and \(\kappa=0\) outside \((-1,1)\).

For \(0<\ell\leq1\), let
\[
 J_\ell=\{j\in\mathbb Z^d:\operatorname{dist}_\infty(\ell j,D)\leq\ell\},
 \qquad
 \phi_j(x)=\prod_{k=1}^d\kappa(x_k/\ell-j_k),
\]
and set
\[
 G_\ell(x)=\sum_{j\in J_\ell}\phi_j(x)^2,
 \qquad
 \psi_j(x)=\phi_j(x)G_\ell(x)^{-1/2}.
\]
The set \(J_\ell\) is finite.  Coordinatewise nearest-integer rounding gives, for every \(x\in D\), an index \(j\in J_\ell\) such that \(\|x/\ell-j\|_\infty\leq1/2\).  Thus \(G_\ell(x)\geq1\) on \(D\), and the same argument gives a fixed positive lower bound on a neighborhood of \(D\).  At any point at most \(3^d\) of the functions \(\phi_j\) are nonzero.  The chain and product rules, applied inductively to \(G_\ell^{-1/2}\), consequently give, for every multi-index \(\nu\),
\[
 \sum_{j\in J_\ell}\psi_j(x)^2=1,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{supp}(\psi_j|_D)
 \subseteq\{x\in D:\|x-\ell j\|_\infty\leq\ell\},
 \qquad
 \sup_{x\in D}|D^\nu\psi_j(x)|\leq C_\nu\ell^{-|\nu|}.
 \tag{1}
\]
All constants in this proof may depend on the fixed tuple \((d,\alpha,\beta,\gamma,L)\), but not on \(n,\ell,h,a,b,x_\circ\), or the signs below.

For \(0<h\leq1\), define an inward-shifted center coordinatewise by
\[
 c_{h,k}=\min\{1-h/2,\max\{h/2,x_{\circ,k}\}\},
 \qquad k=1,\ldots,d,
\]
and put
\[
 w_{h,x_\circ}(x)=\prod_{k=1}^d
 \kappa\!\left(\frac{x_k-c_{h,k}}{h}\right),
 \qquad K_h(x)=w_{h,x_\circ}(x)^2.
 \tag{2}
\]
Because \(|c_{h,k}-x_{\circ,k}|\leq h/2\), one has \(w_{h,x_\circ}(x_\circ)=K_h(x_\circ)=1\).  The active set \(\{x\in D:w_{h,x_\circ}(x)\neq0\}\) has Lebesgue volume at most \((2h)^d\).  This proves the required boundary statement: the center is shifted toward the cube, and intersection of the translated window with \(D\) can only decrease its volume.  No covariate support is deleted.

Let \(\vartheta=(\vartheta_j:j\in J_\ell)\) have independent Rademacher coordinates and, for \(0<\ell\leq h\), define
\[
 F_\vartheta(x)=w_{h,x_\circ}(x)
 \sum_{j\in J_\ell}\vartheta_j\psi_j(x).
 \tag{3}
\]
By (1), independence and centering of the signs, and Cauchy--Schwarz over the at most \(3^d\) active indices,
\[
 \mathbb E_\vartheta F_\vartheta(x)=0,
 \qquad
 \mathbb E_\vartheta F_\vartheta(x)^2=K_h(x),
 \qquad
 |F_\vartheta(x)|\leq B:=3^{d/2},
 \qquad 0\leq K_h(x)\leq1.
 \tag{4}
\]

We record the smoothness estimates in the exact H\"older convention of the core.  If \(s>0\), let \(m=\lceil s\rceil-1\).  Product differentiation in (1)--(3), together with \(\ell\leq h\), gives
\[
 \sup_{x\in D}|D^\nu F_\vartheta(x)|\leq C_s\ell^{-|\nu|},
 \qquad
 \sup_{x\in D}|D^\nu K_h(x)|\leq C_sh^{-|\nu|},
 \qquad |\nu|\leq m+1.
 \tag{5}
\]
For either function \(H\), with \(r=\ell\) for \(F_\vartheta\) and \(r=h\) for \(K_h\), the sup-norm bound and the mean-value theorem on the convex cube imply, for \(|\nu|=m\) and \(\delta=\|x-y\|_\infty\),
\[
 |D^\nu H(x)-D^\nu H(y)|
 \leq C_sr^{-m}\min\{1,\delta/r\}
 \leq C_sr^{-s}\delta^{s-m}.
 \tag{6}
\]
The last inequality uses \(0<s-m\leq1\) and \(\min\{1,z\}\leq z^{s-m}\).  It includes integral \(s\), for which \(s-m=1\).  Equations (5)--(6) prove
\[
 \|F_\vartheta\|_{\mathcal H_d^s}\leq C_s\ell^{-s},
 \qquad
 \|K_h\|_{\mathcal H_d^s}\leq C_sh^{-s},
 \tag{7}
\]
where the notation denotes the maximum of all derivative bounds and the terminal seminorm appearing in the definition of \(\mathcal H_d^s\).

Choose fixed positive \(a_0,b_0\) sufficiently small that
\[
 a_0B\leq\frac1{16},
 \qquad
 b_0\left(B+\frac{a_0}{p}\right)\leq\frac18.
 \tag{8}
\]
For \(0<a\leq a_0\), \(0<b\leq b_0\), \(\varepsilon\in\{-1,1\}\), and a sign vector \(\vartheta\), define
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 e_\vartheta(x)&=p+aF_\vartheta(x),\\
 \mu_{0,\varepsilon,\vartheta}(x)
 &=\frac12+\varepsilon bF_\vartheta(x)
   +\frac{\varepsilon ab}{1-p}K_h(x),\\
 \tau_\varepsilon(x)&=-\frac{\varepsilon ab}{p(1-p)}K_h(x),\\
 \mu_{1,\varepsilon,\vartheta}(x)
 &=\frac12+\varepsilon bF_\vartheta(x)
   -\frac{\varepsilon ab}{p}K_h(x).
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{9}
\]
The last three lines give \(\mu_{1,\varepsilon,\vartheta}-\mu_{0,\varepsilon,\vartheta}=\tau_\varepsilon\) exactly.  Equations (4) and (8) imply
\[
 e_\vartheta\in[5/16,7/16],
 \qquad
 \mu_{0,\varepsilon,\vartheta},\mu_{1,\varepsilon,\vartheta}
 \in[3/8,5/8].
 \tag{10}
\]

We now choose all scales deterministically.  Recall \(S=\alpha+\beta\) and
\(\eta=\{1+d/(2\gamma)+d/(2S)\}^{-1}\).  Set
\[
 \ell=c_\ell n^{-\eta/S},
 \qquad h=\ell^{S/\gamma},
 \qquad a=c_a\ell^\alpha,
 \qquad b=c_b\ell^\beta,
 \tag{11}
\]
where \(0<c_\ell\leq1\), \(0<c_a\leq a_0\), and \(0<c_b\leq b_0\) are fixed below.  By \(\mathrm{ass:below\mbox{-}elbow}\),
\[
 S\leq\frac{d\gamma}{2\gamma+d}<\gamma.
\]
Therefore \(0<\ell\leq h\leq1\).  From (7) and (11),
\[
 a\|F_\vartheta\|_{\mathcal H_d^\alpha}\leq Cc_a,
 \qquad
 b\|F_\vartheta\|_{\mathcal H_d^\beta}\leq Cc_b,
 \tag{12}
\]
and
\[
 ab\|K_h\|_{\mathcal H_d^\beta}
 \leq Cc_ac_b\ell^{S-S\beta/\gamma}\leq Cc_ac_b,
 \qquad
 ab\|K_h\|_{\mathcal H_d^\gamma}
 \leq Cc_ac_b\ell^S h^{-\gamma}=Cc_ac_b.
 \tag{13}
\]
The first inequality in (13) uses \(\gamma>\beta\) and \(0<\ell\leq1\).  Since \(L\geq4\), we may choose the positive constants \(c_a,c_b\), depending only on the fixed parameters, small enough that (10), (12), and (13) imply
\[
 4e_\vartheta\in\mathcal H_d^\alpha(L),\quad
 1\leq4e_\vartheta\leq2,\quad
 \mu_{0,\varepsilon,\vartheta}\in\mathcal H_d^\beta(L),\quad
 \tau_\varepsilon\in\mathcal H_d^\gamma(L),\quad
 \frac18\leq\mu_{a,\varepsilon,\vartheta}\leq\frac78.
 \tag{14}
\]
Thus (14) verifies separately \(\mathrm{ass:propensity\mbox{-}normalization}\), \(\mathrm{ass:propensity\mbox{-}envelope}\), \(\mathrm{ass:propensity\mbox{-}holder}\), \(\mathrm{ass:control\mbox{-}holder}\), \(\mathrm{ass:contrast\mbox{-}holder}\), and \(\mathrm{ass:response\mbox{-}interiority}\).

For each \((\varepsilon,\vartheta)\), construct a full-data law as follows.  Draw \(X\) uniformly on \(D\).  Conditional on \(X=x\), draw \(Y(0)\) and \(Y(1)\) independently as Bernoulli variables with means \(\mu_{0,\varepsilon,\vartheta}(x)\) and \(\mu_{1,\varepsilon,\vartheta}(x)\), draw \(A\) independently of them with success probability \(e_\vartheta(x)\), and set \(Y=AY(1)+(1-A)Y(0)\).  This verifies \(\mathrm{ass:uniform\mbox{-}design}\), \(\mathrm{ass:bernoulli\mbox{-}response}\), \(\mathrm{ass:consistency}\), and \(\mathrm{ass:conditional\mbox{-}exchangeability}\).  Together with (14) and \(\mathrm{def:exact\mbox{-}model}\), every constructed full-data law lies in \(\mathcal P(d,\alpha,\beta,\gamma,L)\).  Let \(\Pi_\varepsilon\) be the uniform prior over these finitely many laws as \(\vartheta\) ranges over \(\{-1,1\}^{J_\ell}\).  Because \(K_h(x_\circ)=1\), the target is constant under this prior and
\[
 \tau_\varepsilon(x_\circ)=-\frac{\varepsilon ab}{p(1-p)}.
 \tag{15}
\]

We next prove exact singleton cancellation and the component inequality.  At a fixed \(x\), abbreviate \(F=F_\vartheta(x)\) and \(K=K_h(x)\).  Replace \((a,\varepsilon b)\) in (9) by real variables \((s,t)\).  In the cell order \((A,Y)=(1,1),(1,0),(0,1),(0,0)\), direct multiplication of the treatment probability and conditional response probability gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 q_{11}(s,t)&=p/2+sF/2+ptF+st(F^2-K)-s^2tKF/p,\\
 q_{10}(s,t)&=p/2+sF/2-ptF-st(F^2-K)+s^2tKF/p,\\
 q_{01}(s,t)&=(1-p)/2-sF/2+(1-p)tF-st(F^2-K)-s^2tKF/(1-p),\\
 q_{00}(s,t)&=(1-p)/2-sF/2-(1-p)tF+st(F^2-K)+s^2tKF/(1-p).
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{16}
\]
These four quantities sum to one.  With
\[
 q_0=(p/2,p/2,(1-p)/2,(1-p)/2),
\]
equation (4) gives, cell by cell and for every \((s,t)\),
\[
 \mathbb E_\vartheta q_z(s,t;x)=q_{0,z}.
 \tag{17}
\]
Thus the two singleton conditional sign-mixture laws are exactly equal, including in the transition part of the localization window.

After reducing \(a_0,b_0\), if necessary, (8)--(10) applied throughout \(|s|\leq a_0,|t|\leq b_0\) give
\[
 \frac12\leq\frac{q_z(s,t;x)}{q_{0,z}}\leq\frac32.
 \tag{18}
\]
This can also be checked directly: the treatment probabilities lie in \([5/16,7/16]\), the response means lie in \([3/8,5/8]\), and comparison of their four products with \(q_0\) gives (18).  Formula (16), \(|F|\leq B\), and \(0\leq K\leq1\) also bound uniformly by a constant \(C_0\) the first \(s\)-derivative, first \(t\)-derivative, and mixed \((s,t)\)-derivative of every ratio in (18).

Fix any locations \(x_1,\ldots,x_r\) and any cell vector \(z=(z_1,\ldots,z_r)\).  Relative to \(q_0^{\otimes r}\), the conditional sign-mixture likelihood is
\[
 M_r(s,t;z)=\mathbb E_\vartheta\prod_{i=1}^r
 \frac{q_{z_i}(s,t;x_i)}{q_{0,z_i}}.
 \tag{19}
\]
The expectation is a finite sum.  The product rule gives at most \(r\) terms in which both derivatives hit one factor and \(r(r-1)\) terms in which they hit distinct factors.  Hence (18) and the derivative bounds imply
\[
 |\partial_s\partial_tM_r(s,t;z)|
 \leq C_1r^2(3/2)^r.
 \tag{20}
\]
At \(s=0\), replacing every \(\vartheta_j\) by \(-\vartheta_j\) replaces \(F_\vartheta\) by \(-F_\vartheta\) and preserves the sign prior.  Inspection of (16) therefore gives \(M_r(0,b;z)=M_r(0,-b;z)\).  The fundamental theorem of calculus first in \(s\) and then in \(t\), followed by (20), yields
\[
 |M_r(a,b;z)-M_r(a,-b;z)|
 \leq\int_0^a\int_{-b}^b
 |\partial_s\partial_tM_r(s,t;z)|\,dt\,ds
 \leq2C_1abr^2(3/2)^r.
 \tag{21}
\]
By (18), both mixture likelihoods in (21) are at least \(2^{-r}\).  If \(Q_{r,+}\) and \(Q_{r,-}\) denote the two conditional cell-mixture laws, the identity
\((\sqrt u-\sqrt v)^2=(u-v)^2/(\sqrt u+\sqrt v)^2\) and (21) give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 H^2(Q_{r,+},Q_{r,-})
 &=\sum_zq_0^{\otimes r}(z)
 \frac{|M_r(a,b;z)-M_r(a,-b;z)|^2}
 {\{\sqrt{M_r(a,b;z)}+\sqrt{M_r(a,-b;z)}\}^2}\\
 &\leq Ca^2b^2r^4(9/2)^r.
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{22}
\]
For \(r=1\), (17) gives \(H^2(Q_{1,+},Q_{1,-})=0\) exactly.  This proves the asserted component estimate without imposing any restriction on how the active frames overlap.

It remains to sum the actual fixed-sample mixture.  Condition on \(X_{1:n}\), as permitted by \(\mathrm{ass:iid\mbox{-}sampling}\).  Retain indices \(i\) for which \(w_{h,x_\circ}(X_i)\neq0\), and join two retained indices when
\(\|X_i-X_j\|_\infty\leq2\ell\).  If the same sign \(\vartheta_k\) appears in both \(F_\vartheta(X_i)\) and \(F_\vartheta(X_j)\), the support statement in (1) implies this edge relation.  Hence distinct connected components depend on disjoint sets of independent signs.  Inactive observations have \(F_\vartheta=K_h=0\) and exactly the baseline cell law.  The conditional mixture of the genuine product law \(P_O^{\otimes n}\) therefore factors over the graph components; no sign is redrawn between observations.

For product laws, Hellinger affinities multiply.  Indeed, this follows by Fubini from the product densities.  Since
\(H^2(P,Q)=2-2\int\sqrt{dP\,dQ}\) and
\(1-\prod_j u_j\leq\sum_j(1-u_j)\) for \(u_j\in[0,1]\), one obtains
\[
 H^2\!\left(\bigotimes_jP_j,\bigotimes_jQ_j\right)
 \leq\sum_jH^2(P_j,Q_j).
 \tag{23}
\]
Let \(N_r\) be the number of components of size \(r\).  Equations (22)--(23) show that the conditional squared Hellinger distance is at most
\[
 Ca^2b^2\sum_{r=2}^nr^4(9/2)^rN_r.
 \tag{24}
\]

We bound the expectation of \(N_r\) directly under the exact uniform product design.  A connected graph on a specified \(r\)-element label set has a spanning tree: starting with one vertex, repeatedly add an edge from the reached set to its nonempty complement.  Root such a tree at the least label and encode it by the parent of each of the other \(r-1\) labels.  This encoding is injective, so there are at most \(r^{r-1}\) such trees.  For a fixed rooted tree, integrate its root over the active set, of volume at most \((2h)^d\), and then integrate each child over a sup-norm ball of radius \(2\ell\) about its parent, of volume at most \((4\ell)^d\).  Independence and \(\mathrm{ass:uniform\mbox{-}design}\) give
\[
 \mathbb E N_r
 \leq\binom nr r^{r-1}(2h)^d(4\ell)^{d(r-1)}.
 \tag{25}
\]
The event on the right of this union bound omits the requirements that the vertices form an entire component and that every child is active, so it is indeed an upper bound.

For \(r\geq1\),
\[
 \log(r!)=\sum_{k=1}^r\log k
 \geq\int_1^r\log x\,dx
 =r\log r-r+1,
\]
and hence \(r!\geq(r/\mathrm e)^r\).  Put \(A_*=9/2\) and \(u=4^dn\ell^d\).  From (25),
\[
 \mathbb E\sum_{r=2}^nr^4A_*^rN_r
 \leq Cnh^d\sum_{r=2}^nr^3(\mathrm e A_*)^r u^{r-1}.
 \tag{26}
\]
If \(\mathrm e A_*u\leq1/2\), then
\[
 \sum_{r=2}^\infty r^3(\mathrm e A_*)^r u^{r-1}
 =(\mathrm e A_*)^2u\sum_{r=2}^\infty r^3(\mathrm e A_*u)^{r-2}
 \leq Cu.
 \tag{27}
\]
Combining (24), (26), and (27) gives
\[
 \mathbb E_XH^2\!\left(
 \mathsf M_+(\,\cdot\mid X_{1:n}),
 \mathsf M_-(\,\cdot\mid X_{1:n})\right)
 \leq Cn^2h^d\ell^da^2b^2.
 \tag{28}
\]
Here \(\mathsf M_\varepsilon=\int P_O^{\otimes n}\,d\Pi_\varepsilon\).  The two mixtures have the same uniform \(X_{1:n}\)-marginal.  Substitution of their joint densities into the defining Hellinger integral and Fubini therefore show that their unconditional squared Hellinger distance equals the left side of (28).  This is a calculation in the original fixed-\(n\) experiment, with neither occupancy conditioning nor Poissonization.

We finally choose \(c_\ell\).  Positivity of all parameters and the definition of \(\eta\) give
\[
 1-\frac{d\eta}{S}\leq0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 S\leq\frac{d\gamma}{2\gamma+d}.
 \tag{29}
\]
Thus \(\mathrm{ass:below\mbox{-}elbow}\) and (11) imply
\[
 n\ell^d=c_\ell^d n^{1-d\eta/S}\leq c_\ell^d
 \qquad(n\geq2).
 \tag{30}
\]
Choose \(c_\ell>0\) so small that \(\mathrm e A_*4^dc_\ell^d\leq1/2\); this verifies the hypothesis of (27), including at equality in (29).  Moreover,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 n^2h^d\ell^da^2b^2
 &=c_a^2c_b^2n^2\ell^{,2S+d+Sd/\gamma}\\
 &=c_a^2c_b^2c_\ell^{,2S+d+Sd/\gamma},
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{31}
\]
because
\[
 \frac{\eta}{S}\left(2S+d+\frac{Sd}{\gamma}\right)
 =\eta\left(2+\frac dS+\frac d\gamma\right)=2.
\]
Decrease the still positive \(c_\ell\), if necessary, so that the right side of (28) is at most \(1/4\).  Finally, (11), (15), and \(\mathrm{def:rate}\) give
\[
 |\tau_+(x_\circ)-\tau_-(x_\circ)|
 =\frac{2ab}{p(1-p)}
 =\frac{2c_ac_bc_\ell^S}{p(1-p)}n^{-\eta}
 =c\rho_n
 \tag{32}
\]
for a fixed \(c>0\).  Taking \(x_\circ=0\) proves every assertion in the theorem.  Because the construction and all constants above are uniform in \(x_\circ\), the identical conclusion also holds at every fixed known \(x_0\in[0,1]^d\).  At the elbow, (29)--(32) remain unchanged and \(\eta=\gamma/(2\gamma+d)\), so the construction has the oracle exponent with no logarithmic factor.

For completeness, the certificate has the advertised minimax consequence.  From \(H^2(\mathsf M_+,\mathsf M_-)\leq1/4\), Cauchy--Schwarz applied to \(|p-q|=|\sqrt p-\sqrt q|(\sqrt p+\sqrt q)\) gives \(\|\mathsf M_+-\mathsf M_-\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\leq1/2\).  Thresholding any Borel estimator at the midpoint of the two constants in (15) then yields
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal P(d,\alpha,\beta,\gamma,L)}
 \mathbb E_P|T-\tau_P(x_\circ)|
 \geq\frac{|\tau_+(x_\circ)-\tau_-(x_\circ)|}{4}
 \{1-\|\mathsf M_+-\mathsf M_-\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\}
 \geq\frac c8\rho_n.
\]
This last reduction uses only that both finite priors are supported on the same exact model established above.

In the requested early-kill case \(d=1\), \(\alpha=\beta=1/8\), and \(\gamma=1\), one has \(S=1/4\), \(\eta=2/7\), \(\ell\asymp n^{-8/7}\), \(h\asymp n^{-2/7}\), and \(a=b\asymp n^{-1/7}\).  Hence \(n\ell\asymp n^{-1/7}\), (17) eliminates every singleton term, (26)--(27) include every component size \(r\geq2\), and \(n^2h\ell a^2b^2\asymp1\).  There is therefore neither an uncancelled singleton contribution nor a macro-scale leakage term.
